description: Hi, I’m Karan, and I’m taking on the Flame in Freefall challenge independently. I’m interested in exploring what microgravity combustion data can teach us about fire safety. I’ll work through the data, develop my ideas, and share the findings in a clear and practical way.
summary: FlameScope turns selected NASA microgravity combustion records into an interactive, source-linked telemetry dashboard. It presents SAFFIRE-I (PSI-98) and FLEX (PSI-69) as separate experiments, keeping original units, time bases, run conditions, data-quality notes, and source-row references visible. A transparent rolling median/MAD screen ranks candidate single-channel departures for human review. It does not label a point as a fire or claim to predict emergencies. With one SAFFIRE-I telemetry workbook and one FLEX run, the current evidence is too limited for a general predictive model. FlameScope makes the evidence inspectable now and shows what calibration, labeled runs, and held-out-run validation are needed before a future fire-safety model could be trusted.
details:
FlameScope is an interactive React and TypeScript dashboard with Node.js data-preparation scripts. It addresses the Flame in Freefall challenge by making NASA combustion measurements easier to explore without losing the experiment context behind each signal.

NASA data represented:

• SAFFIRE-I (PSI-98, record version 4; DOI 10.60555/0t15-1z43): 2,540 timestamped Cygnus observations plus a separate 105-row SAFFIRE sensor stream.

• FLEX (PSI-69, record version 5; DOI 10.60555/mbq8-0451): FLEX-007 / test 20CAL13 droplet, LLUV, and color-camera streams with 141, 177, and 158 timestamped rows.

The dashboard lets a reviewer switch between these investigations and their individual telemetry channels. It displays the reported units, time basis, run context, valid-sample counts, data-quality notes, NASA PSI record, and source-row provenance. SAFFIRE and FLEX streams keep their own clocks; the prototype does not join measurements by row number or imply the experiments are interchangeable.

Processing preserves source order, channel names, reported units, timestamps, missing values, and measured peaks. Rows without usable timestamps are counted and left out of curated time-series views. The pipeline does not smooth, resample, calibrate, or remove statistical outliers. Per-stream quality reports and a source manifest record the selected PSI record and file versions, original filenames, retrieval details, and SHA-256 checksums. Raw source workbooks are not included in the public repository; curated derivatives and provenance are.

For one selected channel, an exploratory rolling median/MAD screen compares a reading with up to 15 preceding valid samples. It requires at least eight baseline samples, highlights an absolute robust score of 3.5 or more, skips windows with zero MAD, and ranks the three largest candidates. Each candidate is linked to its time, value, channel, run context, and source row. A flagged sample may reflect combustion behavior, instrument response, or a data issue. This is a transparent statistical heuristic—not a trained AI classifier, calibrated probability, validated predictor, or operational fire alarm. A flag is not proof of fire, and no flag is not evidence of safety. The available evidence is one SAFFIRE-I telemetry workbook and one FLEX run, so broad predictive claims are not supported.

The practical contribution is traceability: researchers can inspect fire-relevant NASA measurements while seeing what the data can and cannot establish. The next research step is to add independent runs, resolve calibration and clock questions, establish source-reviewed event labels, and validate against simple baselines with whole runs held out. My longer-term interest is to connect AI and physics to quantum computing; only after a reliable classical baseline and sufficient run-level data exist would I compare a small quantum-kernel experiment with matched classical methods. No quantum advantage or predictive performance is claimed here.

Built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Node.js, and Lucide icons. Original project code is MIT-licensed; the selected PSI records identify their data as CC0-1.0. OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex assisted with planning, source analysis, data-processing code, dashboard implementation, documentation, and the demo. The author reviewed the scientific claims and data limitations. FlameScope is an independent participant project; NASA does not endorse it.
